Key Research Thinking Patterns: Homological Resolution via Conic Modules: Establishing non-commutative crepant resolutions by constructing explicit projective resolutions for endomorphism rings of conic modules and analyzing rings of differential operators in positive characteristic.

Topological-Combinatorial Correspondence: Proving that superunitary regions in finite type cluster algebras form regular CW complexes homeomorphic to generalized associahedra, thereby using topological compactness to derive uniform finiteness results for positive integral friezes.

Singular Locus Analysis via Deep Ideals: Characterizing the geometric and algebraic properties of cluster varieties by studying the 'deep locus' defined by the deep ideal D(A), linking its structure to regularity, finite generation, and the distinction between cluster and upper cluster algebras.

Valuative Theta Reciprocity Framework: Deriving bases for global sections of line bundles on partial compactifications by proving valuative independence and reciprocity symmetries for theta functions constructed from positive scattering diagrams and moduli of local systems.
Summary Description: Greg Muller specializes in commutative algebra, algebraic geometry, and cluster algebras, bridging homological methods with combinatorial topology. He establishes non-commutative resolutions of singularities through explicit projective resolutions of conic module endomorphism rings and differential operator rings. His work demonstrates that superunitary regions in cluster algebras are homeomorphic to generalized associahedra, enabling uniform proofs for frieze finiteness. Muller systematically analyzes 'deep points' to characterize variety regularity and the relationship between cluster and upper cluster algebras. Recently, he developed a valuative theta reciprocity framework, proving independence and symmetry for theta functions derived from scattering diagrams, thereby identifying bases for global sections on partial compactifications and linking cluster combinatorics to moduli of local systems.
